name: Detox / slimming teas

lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal blends marketed for cleansing and weight loss, and many rely on senna, a plant whose sennosides are a stimulant laxative. Users drink them to de-bloat and look flatter around the stomach for a short window, such as before an event or photos.

Senna increases fluid and electrolytes in the large bowel and stimulates gut movement, so the scale change largely reflects stool and water loss rather than body fat. A 2015 review of detox diets found no compelling evidence for weight management or toxin elimination, and weight lost on such regimens is typically regained.

paras: People brew the tea for a few days, often timed to an event. It is usually combined with lighter eating during that period.

Reported senna effects are abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea and flatulence, and lower potassium, which can increase digoxin toxicity. Regular use can cause melanosis coli, a brown discoloration of the colon wall. Senna is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and some inflammatory bowel conditions.

angle.text: Users drink detox and slimming teas to de-bloat and drop scale weight quickly before events or photos. The change is typically fluid and gut contents rather than fat, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.

lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal drinks marketed to cleanse the body, reduce bloating and help people slim down. They are sold as loose-leaf blends, tea bags and multi-day "teatox" kits, often with a morning blend and an evening blend, and many are built around senna, a plant-derived stimulant laxative, sometimes alongside herbs such as liquorice root, dandelion root, milk thistle or yellow dock [1][2]. People use them in short courses in the hope of a flatter-looking stomach, a lower number on the scale and a leaner appearance before an event, holiday or photo [3].

Senna glycosides (sennosides) raise fluid and electrolytes in the large bowel and stimulate its movement, and oral products typically produce a bowel movement 6 to 12 hours after a dose, which is why many kits tell users to drink the stronger blend in the evening [1]. Because laxatives act after nutrients have already been absorbed, the weight change they produce reflects mostly temporary loss of stool and water rather than calories [4]. Marketing for these teas, by contrast, tends to speak of toxins being flushed out, a word that reviewers note is rarely defined [5][6].

The category has a short but well-documented commercial history. Influencer-promoted brands such as Flat Tummy Tea and Teami grew rapidly on Instagram in the mid-2010s, and regulators and courts responded between 2014 and 2020: a US class action over senna-based teas, a UK Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) ruling in 2017, a US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) settlement in 2020, and retailer withdrawals in New Zealand [7][3][2][8]. A 2015 review of detox diets in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics found little clinical evidence for them and noted that no randomized controlled trials of commercial detox diets in humans had been conducted [6].

paras: Detox regimens in general claim that toxins stored in fat or the gut are released and eliminated through the skin, urine, feces or breath, and some proponents point to changes in body odor or a sense of lightness as signs it is working [5]. Practices range from juice fasting to colon cleansing, and teas are one of the packaged products in this market. Dietitians and toxicologists quoted in reference sources say the liver and kidneys already handle elimination [5].

Slimming teas are typically sold as multi-week programmes. Reviews by consumer groups and regulators describe blends in which senna leaf is the active laxative component, with other herbs added as supporting ingredients [2]. A "teatox" is usually a 14 or 28 day kit, and brands promote it with photographs of flat stomachs, discount codes and before-and-after images [3][9].

Users commonly describe a flatter abdomen the morning after the evening blend, which is consistent with emptied bowel contents [4]. Supporters describe teatoxes as a motivational reset that kick-starts healthier habits around a particular occasion; sceptics explain reported benefits as short-term calorie restriction, placebo or natural recovery [5][6].

Ideas about internal cleansing have a long history. Reference sources describe the colonic autointoxication theory, the idea that waste in the gut poisons the body, gaining support in the nineteenth century from early biochemistry and microbiology [5]. Walter C. Alvarez's 1919 JAMA article challenged the theory, and by the 1920s colon cleansing was widely regarded by physicians as discredited. Interest revived from the 1970s with the growth of alternative medicine, and later detox language drew on environmental concern about pollution [5].

Senna itself has been used as a laxative plant since at least the 700s AD and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List for constipation and bowel preparation [1]. The packaging of senna as a weight-loss or "cleanse" tea came later. A class action filed in April 2014 against Triple Leaf Tea Inc. in the Northern District of California alleged that its Dieter's Green, Ultra Slim and Super Slimming herbal teas were marketed as weight-loss aids when they were laxatives; a settlement approved in November 2015 required label and website changes and a disclaimer that the teas were not intended as weight-loss aids, without payments to class members [8].

From the mid-2010s, teatox brands built much of their sales on Instagram, with celebrities and reality-television personalities posting product photos and discount codes. Truth in Advertising reported in 2017 that detox companies had used influencers to promote products on Instagram, and that members of the Kardashian family had promoted a leading brand with or without paid-ad disclosures [9].

In a ruling dated 13 September 2017, the UK ASA examined an Instagram post, seen on 22 March 2017, in which television personality Sophie Kasaei promoted Flat Tummy Tea, marketed by Nomad Choice Pty Ltd. The post carried the text "Nothings gonna get you flat the same as this tea will" next to what appeared to be a before-and-after image [9]. The ASA upheld complaints that the ad and the product name implied health benefits, such as reducing water weight, that were not authorised on the EU health-claims register; the advertiser told the ASA it held no scientific data supporting the claims, and the ad was banned in its existing form [3][9].

On 18 September 2019 Facebook and Instagram announced they would remove posts that promote diet or weight-loss products with a commercial offer such as a discount code and make miraculous claims, and would hide some weight-loss and cosmetic-procedure content from users under 18. Coverage of the announcement cited "flat tummy" teas as an example [10]. Instagram's Emma Collins said the company wanted it to be "a positive place for everyone" [10].

On 5 to 6 March 2020 the FTC announced a settlement with Teami, LLC, a Florida seller of teas including a 30 Day Detox Pack, and its co-owners Adi Halevy and Yogev Malul. The FTC alleged that the company marketed its teas as causing rapid and substantial weight loss and as able to fight cancer cells, reduce migraines and unclog arteries, and that more than $15 million of sales were driven largely by paid Instagram endorsements without adequate disclosure [7].

The proposed order barred unsupported weight-loss and health claims and required clear disclosure of paid connections, plus a system to monitor endorsers. A $15.2 million judgment was partially suspended on payment of $1 million, reflecting the defendants' financial condition [7]. On the same day FTC staff sent warning letters about unclear disclosures to ten people, including entertainers Cardi B, Jordin Sparks and Alexa PenaVega and model Brittany Renner [7].

Senna glycosides are dimeric anthraquinones thought to increase fluid and electrolyte content in the large bowel and to stimulate peristalsis through the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, though the exact mechanism is not entirely clear [1]. Other anthraquinone laxatives include cascara, buckthorn and aloe, with onset around 6 to 10 hours [4].

Because stimulant laxatives act in the colon after the small intestine has absorbed nutrients, body-weight effects reflect primarily temporary loss of water rather than energy, according to reference descriptions of laxative use for weight loss [4]. Senna is sold over the counter in the United States and by pharmacy in other countries; Ex-Lax and Senokot are among the brand names [1].

Reported effects of senna include abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence and discolored urine; regular use can cause melanosis coli, a brown pigmentation of the colon wall seen on colonoscopy, and senna may increase digoxin toxicity by lowering potassium [1]. Contraindications include intestinal obstruction, acute intestinal inflammation, ulcerative colitis, appendicitis and abdominal pain of unknown origin [1]. Older concerns about colon damage and dependence are described as no longer supported by evidence, although long-term human data are limited [1].

Laxative misuse more broadly can cause dehydration, low blood pressure, fainting and acid-base and electrolyte imbalances that can be fatal; laxative misuse is also described in people with eating disorders [4]. Consumer NZ reported in 2020 that prolonged senna use has been linked to liver injury, electrolyte disturbances, heart-rhythm changes and laxative dependency, that liquorice root can interact with medicines including birth control, and that yellow dock contains oxalic acid, associated in reported cases with kidney stones and kidney failure [2]. Massey University's Dr Andrew Dickson said detox products "can be toxic if people consume them in excessive doses" [2].
A 2022 review of fad diets says limited evidence supports their proposed claims and that some carry health risks [11].

Because the laxative effect comes after nutrient absorption, the weight change from a senna tea is mostly stool and fluid, and it returns when normal eating and drinking resume [4]. Detox regimens in general are reported to produce short-term weight loss through calorie restriction, followed by regain [5]. For users aiming at a flatter-looking abdomen for an occasion, this short-lived change in bowel contents and water is the effect on offer [4][3].
The ASA's 2017 ruling recorded that the advertiser said it had no scientific data supporting its claims [3], and Consumer NZ found no reliable evidence that diet teas aid weight loss or detoxing [2].

In the UK, the ASA applied the EU rule that only authorised health claims may be used in food advertising and found that even the product name "Flat Tummy Tea" counted as a health claim [3]. In the US, regulation of the teas as dietary supplements has been mostly through consumer-protection actions on advertising claims, as in the FTC's Teami order [7] and the Triple Leaf class action [8].

In New Zealand, senna's sennosides are a pharmacy-only medicine, so companies need consent to advertise or sell them; selling without consent can bring a fine of up to NZ$100,000. In January 2020 Consumer NZ reported that Healtheries withdrew three teas and stopped using senna, and that Countdown, Foodstuffs and several health-food brands removed senna teas from sale [2].

The Mayo Clinic's Katherine Zeratsky said in 2012 there is little evidence that detox diets remove toxins [5]. The British Dietetic Association has criticised detox as a marketing term [5]. Proponents describe the teas as a gentle cleanse and a way to start healthier habits.

Sense about Science in the UK reported in 2009 that most detox product companies it contacted offered no evidence for their claims [5]. Toxicologist Alan Boobis of Imperial College London has said the body's own detoxification systems are sophisticated [5]. In their 2015 review, Klein and Kiat concluded that there is no compelling evidence that detox diets aid weight management or toxin elimination and recommended independent regulatory review of such products [5][6]. Consumer NZ quotes Otago University's Professor Jim Mann as strongly advising against diet or detox teas [2].

No studies found on slimming teas as a product category. Broader research includes the 2015 critical review of detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management [6], which reported small studies with methodological limitations, and a 2022 review of fad diets [11]. Senna's laxative effect is established in medical use for constipation and bowel preparation [1].
